harness: opencode 1.18.4 `opencode run`, one disposable git worktree per run, one generated permission config per run. NOT the Agent-tool harness the other records in this directory used -- see `harness_deltas` before comparing anything here to them.
scope: all 6 cases x {with_skill, without_skill} = 12 runs, one attempt each, opencode/big-pickle at variant=high.
harness_deltas: Prompt rewritten: `/issue-triage 307 --dry-run` becomes a skill-tool instruction. opencode resolves slash commands from .opencode/command/, not from skills, so the literal prompt in evals.json invokes nothing.

Fixture paths made absolute. With them relative, a baseline run resolved `evals/fixtures/issue-307.json` against $HOME, found nothing, and silently webfetched the live issue #307 -- reading today's thread instead of the frozen report. That run was discarded and webfetch is now denied so the failure is loud.
Baseline arm built by deleting SKILL.md and references/ from the run's worktree; evals/ stays so the fixtures remain readable.

check_no_writes.py cannot scan an opencode transcript directly: the `skill` tool inlines all of SKILL.md, and SKILL.md contains the string `issue_write` in the sentence forbidding it, so every with_skill run fails on the skill's own prohibition. Runs are screened against a distilled tool-call log (tool name + input, never output) instead. All 12 PASS.

gh CLI was authenticated with `repo` scope but no run invoked it; opencode had no MCP servers configured. The Agent-tool records had GitHub MCP available, so the two harnesses differ in reach. Nothing here confirms an issue's live state.

compare.py cannot ingest this record properly. It keys runs on (case, model, effort) and has no concept of an `arm`, so it sees two entries per case, warns 'duplicate run ... keeping the first', and silently drops every without_skill run. It also prints 0 tokens and $0.000 here: this record deliberately carries `tokens_uncached` and `tokens_step_sum` rather than a single `tokens` field, because neither number means what `tokens` means in the Agent-tool records. Comparing this file to those with compare.py is not currently meaningful; read it directly.

pricing_basis.note: opencode reports cost 0 on every step for opencode/big-pickle, so there is no dollar figure to compare against the Claude records. Recorded as 0 rather than estimated.
pricing_basis.token_caveat: opencode reports per-step totals that re-count the cached prefix each step. `tokens_step_sum` is that number and is NOT comparable to the token counts in the Agent-tool records; `tokens_uncached` (input + output + reasoning + cache-write) is the closer analogue. On case 3 the two differ by 20x.

notes: Provider instability shaped the run: `No provider available` (HTTP 401, flagged isRetryable:false) killed 3 of 12 runs at 3-way concurrency and 5 of 12 at 2-way. Every run here is sequential with backoff retry. Three runs needed one retry each. Headline: with_skill 29/42 assertions, without_skill 25/42 -- a 4-assertion gap that is much narrower than the Opus/Sonnet/Haiku spread in the Agent-tool records, and it inverts on two cases. Read the per-case notes rather than the totals: the skill's value shows up as evidence quality (with_skill executed code in 5 of 6 cases, the baseline in 1 of 6) and as never drafting a close, while the baseline drafted comments announcing closes on 7 issues across cases 3 and 6. But the with_skill run botched the one rule the skill states most explicitly -- case 6's batch selection -- while the baseline got it right, and case 1's with_skill run reached a worse verdict than the baseline. Single attempt per cell, and case 1 varied between verdicts A and D across harness iterations, so treat every per-case number as one sample, not a measurement.

An unmerged branch is not a fix, and treating it as one is the more dangerous error of the two -- it would have told the reporter their bug was handled. runs.notes: Ties the with_skill run on score while doing something materially different, which is a sign this case's assertions are too loose -- exactly the failure mode the results README flags. It executed nothing at all, yet accounted for both symptom halves and offered a concrete mechanism for each, so it passes the same four assertions. It then recommended closing as duplicate of #210 and drafted a comment ending 'Closing as duplicate of #210.' Its account of the disappearance (add_periodic_task never syncing post-startup) is a real design limitation and arguably a better answer than the with_skill run's 'could not determine' -- but it is unverified, and no assertion here can tell a verified explanation from a plausible one.
